hours_src.what: The example vehicle. Mazda Technical Service Bulletin 01-014/16 (last issued 09/22/2016; 2014-16 Mazda3, 2013-16 CX-5 and 2014-16 Mazda6 with SKYACTIV-G 2.0 or 2.5): 'Operation Number / Labor Hours: XXM3WBRX / 0.3 Hrs.', part PE20-18-100A Ignition Coil, quantity '1, 2, 3, or 4'. A manufacturer warranty time, the low end of what a shop bills. It is not a pure one-coil time: the one 0.3 hour figure covers swapping the suspect coil to another cylinder to confirm it, then replacing the defective coil or coils (one to four), and the bulletin adds 'Additional diagnostic time cannot be claimed for this repair'. So one coil cannot take longer than 0.3 hour on Mazda's schedule

finding: There is no live range for a one-coil job yet (the site's existing $100-$700 range is for the coil job in general and is checked in the full-set file). Built totals for ONE coil (one coil + the stated hours x $120-$160 per hour, the national middle rate used for this arithmetic): economy 2015 Mazda3 2.0L $81-$226; midsize 2024 Ford Explorer 2.3L $64-$199; truck 2024 Ford Ranger 2.3L $178-$231; luxury 2024 Lincoln Corsair 2.0L $112-$154. Across the four that is roughly $65-$230 before diagnosis. A supportable live range for one coil on a four-cylinder would be about $65-$230; it should not be read as covering six- and eight-cylinder or European luxury engines, which were not built here. The outside estimates sit at or above the top of that: Jerry $142-$234 for one coil, RepairPal $238-$320 (number of coils not stated), J.D. Power $100-$300 for a single conventional coil and $200-$600 per coil on coil-on-plug engines. The built totals run lower mainly because every labor time here is a manufacturer warranty time (the low end of what shops bill), no diagnosis fee is included, and two of the four examples use a genuine coil with a $26.00 list price. How solid the labor times are: all four are manufacturer-stated times for the example vehicle, but none is a bare 'replace one coil' line. Ford TSB 26-2210 words its one-coil operations 'Retrieve DTCs; Inspect Date Code On Related Ignition Coil(s); Replace One Ignition Coil': 0.4 Hrs on the 2024-2025 Explorer 2.3L, 0.6 Hrs on the 2024 Ranger 2.3L and 0.8 Hrs on the 2024-2025 Escape/Corsair 2.0L. That includes reading the stored codes and the date code on top of the coil, which is quick, but it means the pure swap is at most those times. The same bulletin gives one-coil times of 0.3 to 0.5 Hrs for the Maverick 2.0L, Mustang 2.3L, Bronco 2.3L, Bronco Sport and Escape 1.5L, so 0.3 to 0.8 hour is Ford's whole band for one coil on a four-cylinder. Mazda TSB 01-014/16 allows a single 0.3 hour for swap-testing and replacing anywhere from one to four coils on the 2014-16 Mazda3, with no extra diagnostic time allowed: a manufacturer time for the example car, but looser than a one-coil line and it includes the swap test. Because the low and high hours are the same warranty figure in every class, real shop labor will usually come out higher: many shops bill a half-hour or one-hour minimum, and J.D. Power's general guide says the job 'can vary from 0.5 to 2 hours'. No general guide was used to set any high. Caveats on parts: the Ford bulletin's replacement coil P2GZ-12029-A lists at only $26.00, while the earlier coil for the same 2.3L engine (JX6Z-12029-B) lists at $135.45, and the catalog does not say which build takes which; the Explorer range therefore spans both ($16.37 to $135.45), the Ranger uses only the coil the catalog lists for it ($106.25 new at a retailer, $135.45 list), and the Corsair uses only P2GZ-12029-A ($16.37 to $26.00), which makes the luxury example the cheapest job here and unrepresentative of six-cylinder or European luxury cars. No aftermarket-brand coil was found for P2GZ-12029-A, so the Explorer and Corsair lows are the genuine coil at an online discount price on a page stating New condition. For the Mazda3 the dealer catalog page shows $178.32 and $133.71 without labelling them, the retailer's single-coil listing ($44.95) does not print a condition or engine (the same seller's set page for the 2014-2018 Mazda 3 2.0L is listed as new), and the Ranger catalog page likewise shows two unlabelled prices. Dealer-catalog prices are per coil without the word 'each'. Confidence is set to medium by the rule (a manufacturer time for every example vehicle and at least two parts sources per class), with the reservations above: the times include a code read or swap test, the Mazda time covers up to four coils, and the luxury example is a four-cylinder with an unusually cheap coil. Not covered: engines where the intake manifold must come off to reach the rear coils (many transverse V6s), six- and eight-cylinder engines, and older engines with a single coil pack and plug wires.
extras: A quote usually adds a diagnosis fee, because the shop first has to confirm which coil has failed; that is not in these figures. Many shops bill a minimum labor charge of half an hour or an hour even for a quick job. The spark plug in the same cylinder is often replaced at the same time, and the coil boot if it is cracked or oil-soaked. A valve cover gasket may be added if oil is found in the plug well. On a high-mileage engine shops often recommend replacing all the coils when one fails, which multiplies the parts cost by the number of cylinders. Shop supplies and sales tax are extra. A misfire that has been driven on for a long time can damage the catalytic converter, which is a separate and much larger repair.
